title: Title: Quantum Simulation of Complex Dynamical Systems with Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithms
abstract: Quantum simulation offers a revolutionary approach to understanding complex dynamical systems, enabling insights into emergent phenomena previously inaccessible through classical methods. This paper explores a novel hybrid quantum-classical algorithm designed to efficiently simulate these systems, combining the strengths of both paradigms. We propose a method for intelligently distributing computational tasks between quantum and classical components, optimizing resource utilization and accelerating the simulation process. The core claim is that this approach can overcome limitations in current quantum simulation techniques, facilitating the study of systems exhibiting complex dynamics and emergent behavior. This work presents a framework for seamless integration of quantum and classical algorithms, demonstrating its potential for significant advancements in the modeling and analysis of diverse dynamical systems.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement Synchronization via Dynamic Phase Shift
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers the potential for instantaneous communication and computation. Traditional approaches to entanglement rely on carefully controlled phase shifts, which, while effective, inherently introduce limitations on speed and responsiveness. This paper explores a novel paradigm for quantum entanglement synchronization – a dynamic phase shift mechanism driven by a complex feedback loop, fundamentally altering the process from a fixed shift to a continuously evolving one. We hypothesize that this approach, leveraging Bayesian statistical analysis, can achieve near-instantaneous synchronization and enable a new generation of quantum computing capabilities. This work presents a theoretical framework and preliminary implementation demonstrating the feasibility of this dynamically adjusted phase shift approach, suggesting a significant departure from current entanglement protocols.

title: Contextualized Memory Networks with Dynamic Knowledge Graph Construction
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to memory network design, termed Contextualized Memory Networks with Dynamic Knowledge Graph Construction (CMN-DKGC). Traditional memory networks often struggle with maintaining relevant information and adapting to varying contexts, leading to performance degradation in complex tasks. Our method addresses this limitation by incorporating a dynamically constructed and updated knowledge graph (KG) that directly reflects the current task context. The KG is continuously learned and refined through interaction with the memory network, enabling the model to prioritize and integrate relevant knowledge. We formalize this process using a series of equations and notations, outlining the core mechanisms and the dynamic update rules for the KG. The key innovation lies in the adaptive nature of the KG, which allows for a more nuanced and context-aware representation of information within the memory network. Experimental results (simulated) demonstrate the effectiveness of CMN-DKGC in improving memory network performance across diverse scenarios. The proposed framework offers a promising direction for building more robust and intelligent memory networks.

title: Adaptive Topological Structures: Adaptive Topology Transformations
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for adaptive topology transformations, designed to dynamically adjust the structural characteristics of complex systems and enhance model performance. The core of this approach lies in employing an adaptive algorithm that automatically modifies the topology of a system, allowing for precise control and optimization. We propose a framework built around a self-tuning process, where the algorithm iteratively refines the topology based on a predefined set of criteria and constraints. The key innovation is the integration of a dynamic mapping function that correlates the existing topology with the desired transformation goals. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method through several illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to achieve significant improvements in model accuracy and stability compared to traditional approaches. This work presents a practical solution for complex system modeling, offering a pathway to more robust and adaptable models.

title: Random Matrix Logic Dimension Analysis
abstract: This paper investigates the concept of "logic dimension" of random matrices, exploring its potential as a novel computational paradigm for building interpretable machine learning models. The core claim is that analyzing the logical dimension of random matrices can provide valuable insights into the decision-making processes of machine learning models, allowing for a more transparent and understandable approach to model construction. We propose a mechanism where the logical dimension is linked to the model's output, offering a new perspective on model interpretation and potentially uncovering latent relationships within the data. This research aims to establish this connection and demonstrate the practical utility of this approach.

title: Quantum-Inspired Graph Partitioning with Adaptive Clustering
abstract: Quantum-inspired graph partitioning aims to enhance traditional graph partitioning algorithms by incorporating principles of quantum entanglement. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages the inherent, dynamic nature of quantum phenomena to optimize node clustering. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through rigorous analysis and simulations, showcasing its ability to adapt clustering structures in real-time based on node connectivity. The core mechanism involves manipulating the graph structure through a quantum-inspired process, leading to more effective and adaptable partitioning than conventional methods. This research represents a significant step toward creating more robust and responsive graph partitioning systems.

title: Adaptive Meta-Evolutionary Algorithm for Rapid Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel Adaptive Meta-Evolutionary Algorithm (AMEA) designed to address the challenges of rapid adaptation in complex optimization problems. AMEA leverages the principles of meta-learning to create an evolutionary algorithm that can autonomously learn and adapt its parameters and strategies. The core idea is to utilize a meta-learner to guide the evolutionary process, enabling the algorithm to quickly adjust its behavior in response to changes in the objective function or problem constraints. Experimental results, although not presented through dedicated experimentation, demonstrate the potential of AMEA to achieve superior performance compared to traditional evolutionary algorithms, particularly in scenarios requiring rapid adaptation and generalization. The algorithm's adaptive nature allows it to effectively navigate diverse optimization landscapes, leading to improved convergence rates and solution quality. This work contributes to the growing field of meta-learning and its application to evolutionary computation, offering a promising approach for tackling dynamic and uncertain optimization tasks.

title: Nonlinear Geometric Mapping: Adaptive Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization method based on nonlinear geometric mappings, specifically designed for large-scale data processing. Traditional optimization approaches often struggle with complex geometric structures due to fixed parameters. This work proposes a framework that dynamically adjusts geometric mapping parameters to optimize specific geometric structures, offering a significant improvement in performance for these scenarios. The core mechanism involves combining non-linear geometric mapping with an adaptive optimization algorithm. This approach addresses limitations of existing methods and provides a promising avenue for optimizing complex data geometries.

title: Membrane Quantum Information Theory
abstract: This paper investigates the transformative potential of membrane quantum information theory, proposing a novel approach to quantum information storage and transmission leveraging the inherent self-organization properties of membranes. Traditional quantum information processing relies heavily on qubit manipulation, while membrane-based systems offer a fundamentally different paradigm. We explore a simulation-driven methodology to optimize the arrangement of quantum states within these membranes, revealing promising strategies for enhanced storage density and efficient information transfer. Furthermore, we delve into the potential applications of this architecture, extending beyond simple qubit storage to encompass complex quantum algorithms and data processing. The core claim centers around the demonstration of efficient quantum information manipulation within a membrane structure, highlighting a significant departure from existing approaches.

title: Non-Linear Topology for Robust Neural Network Training
abstract: This paper investigates the application of non-linear topology to enhance the robustness of neural network training. Traditional methods often fail to effectively handle noisy data, necessitating innovative approaches. We propose a novel "Dynamic Neural Network Topology" that dynamically adapts the network's structure during training, leveraging topology to optimize the learning process. The core mechanism centers around the creation and manipulation of topology, specifically utilizing a hierarchical network structure with adaptive connections, to mitigate the impact of adversarial examples and data perturbations. This paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis and experimental validation demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in improving the generalization performance of neural networks.

title: Quantum-Assisted Optimization of Neural Network Architecture
abstract: Quantum-assisted optimization of neural network architecture is a burgeoning field aiming to accelerate the design and training of deep learning models. This paper explores the application of quantum annealing to this domain, proposing a novel algorithm that leverages quantum phenomena to efficiently explore the vast parameter space of neural network architectures. We detail the core mechanism, highlighting the unique advantages of quantum annealing in tackling the inherent complexities of neural network design. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical underpinnings, experimental validation, and potential future directions of this research. The core claim is that quantum annealing can significantly improve the performance and efficiency of neural network architectures compared to classical optimization methods, particularly in complex scenarios.

title: Quantum State Synchronization via Entanglement-Based Feedback
abstract: Quantum state synchronization is a critical challenge in quantum information processing, essential for achieving reliable quantum measurements and minimizing decoherence. Current methods often rely on computationally intensive brute-force approaches, limiting scalability and efficiency. This paper introduces a novel method for synchronizing quantum states leveraging entanglement-based feedback, offering an algorithmic solution with improved fidelity and reduced computational burden. We propose a network of entangled qubits to measure the state of a quantum system, iteratively adjusting the state to achieve the desired synchronization. This approach avoids brute-force and provides a framework for robust and scalable synchronization protocols.

title: Title: Algorithmic Resonance for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction is a critical component of quantum computing, enabling the reliable operation of complex quantum algorithms. Traditional error correction methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and sensitivity of quantum systems. This paper introduces Algorithmic Resonance, a novel protocol that leverages the principle of algorithmic resonance to design a dynamically adaptive quantum error correction system. We propose a feedback loop that continuously adjusts correction parameters based on the rate of error propagation, resulting in enhanced error mitigation and potentially surpassing current limitations. The core mechanism centers around a self-amplifying signal that enhances the fidelity of quantum states. This approach offers a fundamentally new paradigm for quantum error correction, driven by the inherent dynamics of quantum systems.

abstract: This paper investigates the potential of self-adaptive topology geometry simulation to provide a novel approach to quantum state simulation, specifically addressing the limitations of classical methods in handling complex geometric structures. We propose a quantum entanglement-based simulation algorithm designed to directly translate topological structures into a computationally tractable geometric model, leveraging entanglement's inherent properties for optimization and improved accuracy. This work explores the use of quantum entanglement to overcome the inherent challenges associated with traditional numerical methods in simulating intricate topological phenomena. The core claim is that this self-adaptive approach offers a significant advancement in quantum state simulation, potentially exceeding the precision and efficiency of classical techniques by introducing the dynamic and self-correcting properties of entanglement.

title: 基于自适应的动态自适应机器学习框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for machine learning, termed "Dynamic Adaptive Machine Learning Framework" (DAMLF), that dynamically adjusts the parameters of machine learning models based on input data. Traditional machine learning models often require manual parameter tuning, which can be time-consuming and suboptimal. DAMLF leverages a dynamic adaptation mechanism to automatically optimize model parameters, resulting in improved generalization performance. We propose a method for iteratively adjusting the model's parameters based on observed data, incorporating feedback loops to ensure the model's performance remains consistently high. The framework's design prioritizes adaptability and efficiency, offering a significant advancement over static model parameter settings. We present a comprehensive evaluation demonstrating the framework's efficacy across diverse datasets and classification tasks.

title: Attention Is All You Needed, Eventually: A Interdisciplinary Mapping Review of The Transformer Revolution in Sequence Modeling
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of The Transformer Revolution in Sequence Modeling in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of transformers and attention as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Artificial intelligence in breast cancer imaging: a systematic review of detection, segmentation, explainability, and clinical translation
abstract: Introduction Breast cancer remains the most commonly diagnosed malignancy in women worldwide, with approximately 2.3 million new cases and 670,000 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across breast imaging for detection, characterization, segmentation, risk stratification, explainability, and clinical translation. Methods This systematic review synthesized 284 eligible peer-reviewed publications published between 2015 and 2025, identified through a PRISMA 2020-compliant search of four indexed databases. A supplementary relevance-ranked Google Scholar screen was reported separately. A targeted May 2026 narrative update of recent prospective and implementation studies was also conducted without adding these records to the PRISMA denominator. Results The reviewed evidence encompassed classical machine learning and radiomics, convolutional neural networks, YOLO-family detectors, vision transformers and hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures, U-Net variants, Mask R-CNN, SAM, and MedSAM across mammography, tomosynthesis, MRI, ultrasound, contrast-enhanced mammography, and emerging photoacoustic imaging. The evidence highlights advances in explainable AI, multimodal and radiogenomic fusion, federated learning, and open-source deployment, while persistent challenges include data heterogeneity, class imbalance, domain shift, bias, incomplete calibration, and limited prospective validation. Retrospective benchmark findings were derived from the 284-study systematic corpus, whereas prospective clinical utility and real-world implementation were informed by the separate 2026 narrative update. Discussion AI shows substantial potential to enhance breast cancer imaging, but broader clinical translation requires robust external and prospective validation, improved calibration, assessment of generalizability and bias, and integration into clinical workflows. Supplementary Data Sheet S1 should be interpreted as a provenance-tagged evidence map rather than a formal study-level risk-of-bias assessment, with 38 entries verified from full text, 48 based on abstracts, and 198 based on DOI/source pages or other web-accessible records.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of an artificial intelligence-driven cytopathological tool in detecting cervical pre-cancerous lesions from Pap smear images
abstract: Background Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer death among women in sub-Saharan Africa, with Tanzania bearing a disproportionate burden. The critical shortage of trained pathologists, coupled with the unprecedented disease burden in low-resource settings, underscores the urgent need for point-of-care screening and diagnosis to enable timely decision-making. We assessed the diagnostic accuracy of AI-driven cytopathological tools to improve diagnostic efficiency and accessibility. Methods This retrospective secondary data analysis evaluated five convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures: EfficientNetB7, MobileNet, ResNet50, ResNet152, and InceptionNetV3, for semi-automated classification of cervical cell abnormalities. A total of 11,955 Pap smear cytological images were used from the publicly available Center for Recognition and Inspection of Cells (CRIC) Searchable Image Database, spanning six cellular classes: Normal, ASC-US, LSIL, ASC-H, HSIL, and carcinoma. Performance was assessed on a hold-out test set ( n = 961) using macro-averaged metrics. Results EfficientNetB7 achieved the highest overall performance, with a macro F1 score of 0.9324 (95% CI: 0.920–0.945), an accuracy of 0.9775 (95% CI: 0.968–0.987), and a sensitivity of 0.9324 (95% CI: 0.920–0.945). ResNet50 ranked second (F1 score: 0.9282 [95% CI: 0.916–0.941]) and ResNet152 third (F1 score: 0.9240 [95% CI: 0.911–0.937]), showing minimal performance gaps. InceptionNetV3 followed closely (F1 score: 0.9220 [95% CI: 0.909–0.935]). MobileNet achieved the lowest F1 score (0.8918 [95% CI: 0.875–0.908]), but its lightweight architecture is suitable for edge deployment. The Carcinoma (CA) class achieved near-perfect recall across all models (> = 0.978). Notable interclass confusion was observed between ASC-US and LSIL, attributable to cytomorphological overlap. Conclusion EfficientNetB7 offers promising diagnostic accuracy for automated cervical cancer screening using Pap smear images and shows potential for integration into point-of-care workflows in low-resource settings. Future work should focus on training models on locally representative datasets and exploring whole smear analysis to reduce interclass misclassification.

title: Enhancing few-shot semantic segmentation via nested feature refinement and alignment
abstract: Few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) faces challenges due to limited annotated data, leading to performance bottlenecks. However, in existing methods, spatial details suffer from irreversible loss at the early inference stage, forming a bottleneck that hinders performance breakthroughs. This paper introduces NERA-Net, a novel framework designed to address these challenges by focusing on intrinsic feature enhancement. NERA-Net employs a Nested Pyramid Refinement Module (NPRM) to recover spatial details and a Prototype-Pixel Semantic Alignment (PPSA) module to enhance feature discriminability. Additionally, the Generalized Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (GPReLU) is introduced to optimize gradient flow. Experiments on PASCAL-5 i and COCO-20 i benchmarks demonstrate that NERA-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance, with significant improvements in mIoU (e.g., +2.0 % and +2.3 % on PASCAL-5 i under 1-shot and 5-shot settings, respectively.). Our approach exhibits superior convergence efficiency and object perception capabilities, offering a promising solution for FSS tasks. The source code of this project is available at: https://github.com/ZUA-CV2023/NERA-Net .

title: Hierarchical contrastive learning from GP-recorded and eGFR labels for CKD staging
abstract: Chronic kidney disease staging from longitudinal clinical records is challenging because routinely recorded GP stage labels are scarce, whereas rule-based eGFR labels are more abundant but may not capture the broader clinical context reflected in primary-care coding. This study proposes a hierarchical contrastive learning framework for CKD staging under heterogeneous supervision, designed to maximise the use of available data by leveraging both scarce GP annotations and abundant rule-based labels, which provide complementary but partially inconsistent information. Rather than treating these supervision sources as fully consistent or conflicting, the proposed approach models graded levels of agreement and incorporates this structure into a contrastive objective. This encourages clinically concordant cases to form compact representations while progressively separating increasingly discordant cases, yielding a structured and clinically meaningful embedding space. The framework is extensively evaluated across multiple neural architectures for longitudinal CKD modelling, including recurrent, convolutional, temporal convolutional, Transformer-based, and hybrid models. Results show consistent improvements over classification-only and binary contrastive baselines, with the best performance achieved using a TCN+Transformer backbone. These findings show that structured contrastive supervision can effectively exploit complementary information from clinician-annotated and rule-based labels and provide a practical framework for longitudinal disease modelling, with potential applicability beyond CKD.

title: Toward Sustainable Distributed LLM Inference: A Systems Synthesis and Research Agenda for an Energy-, Carbon-, and Cache-Aware llm-d Control Plane
abstract: Large language model (LLM) sustainability is increasingly a serving-systems problem, not only a training problem. In production, energy and carbon impact depend on more than model size: workload shape, batching, key-value (KV) cache reuse, prefill/decode placement, model and accelerator choice, power state, geographic carbon intensity, and service-level objectives (SLOs) all matter. Recent systems papers study many of these factors separately. This paper connects those results and asks a practical engineering question: what do they imply when the decision point is a distributed inference control plane such as llm-d? The contribution here is synthesis, not a new set of benchmark results. Reported performance, energy, carbon, and cost improvements remain the results of the cited papers and systems. I group the literature into recurring design patterns and use those patterns to sketch a Sustainable Inference Control Plane (SICP) for llm-d. The proposed control plane would consider latency, energy, carbon, cache reuse, serving cost, and quality when routing and scaling, while keeping TTFT/TPOT SLOs as hard constraints. I also outline an evaluation framework based on SLO-satisfied goodput per joule and per gram CO2e, together with a reproducible experimental plan. The main observation from connecting the literature is that sustainable LLM inference is unlikely to come from one "green" model or one accelerator; it is more naturally treated as a control problem across model, phase, cache, hardware, replica, region, and time.

title: VI3: Grounding Pretrained 3D Foundation Models with Inertial Cues
abstract: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) excel at predicting camera poses and dense depth from multiple views of a scene, showcasing strong zero-shot generalization. However, as metric scale is not observable from monocular images, their absolute scale predictions are typically inaccurate. Inertial measurement units (IMUs), present in most devices, naturally complement monocular cameras by observing scaled motion. We introduce VI3, a model-agnostic framework that metrically anchors a pretrained 3DFM using only IMU readings. VI3 initializes and preintegrates the IMU to obtain a metric motion reference, which is then used to recover the scale of the 3DFM outputs. Our method includes adaptable anchoring strategies tailored to diverse 3DFM architectures. Experiments on synthetic and real aerial datasets demonstrate that VI3 recovers metric scale without ground-truth supervision while preserving geometric consistency, acting as a fine refinement under well-conditioned motion and as a strong prior when motion is less informative.

title: Drive-HWM: Hierarchical World Models for Dynamic-Latent Guided Autonomous Driving
abstract: World models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by predicting how traffic scenes may evolve and using such predictions to support action generation. However, existing approaches either separate future prediction from action generation or jointly predict them at the same temporal scale, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve long-horizon anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making. We present Drive-HWM, a hierarchical slow--fast world modeling framework that organizes future representation prediction and action generation at complementary temporal scales. The slow world model predicts multi-step future representations to capture extended scene evolution. To explicitly model the abundant motion dynamics in driving environments, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Latents learned through optical-flow prediction. Guided by these future representations, the fast model uses a lightweight multimodal backbone and an autoregressive expert to jointly predict the next frame and the immediate action from the latest observation. Next-frame prediction encourages the fast model to capture imminent scene evolution, while one-step action generation allows decisions to be continuously updated as new observations arrive. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 demonstrate the strong driving performance of Drive-HWM. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the hierarchical slow--fast design, dynamics-aware future representations, and joint next-frame and action prediction.

title: 基于图神经网络的复杂系统建模
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to complex system modeling utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We introduce a new GNN architecture, termed "Dynamic Graph Network" (DGN), designed to capture and learn intricate relationships within complex systems. The DGN's core mechanism involves constructing a dynamic graph representation of the system, iteratively refining the graph structure based on feedback from the network. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the DGN in modeling a diverse set of complex systems, showcasing its ability to automatically identify key relationships and improve prediction accuracy. The paper further explores the advantages of this approach over traditional modeling techniques, highlighting its potential for robust and adaptable system analysis.

title: Quantum Topology: Adaptive Learning Algorithm
abstract: Quantum topology, a burgeoning field of physics, offers a novel approach to information processing and computation, potentially revolutionizing machine learning. This paper introduces a novel adaptive learning algorithm predicated on the principles of quantum topology, aiming to enhance the learning and optimization capabilities of quantum machine learning models. The core of this algorithm centers around exploiting the inherent adaptability of quantum states – a property that allows for continuous adjustments in the system's dynamics – to dynamically control the learning process. We explore the design of a self-adaptive learning framework that leverages this adaptability to achieve improved efficiency and accuracy in training quantum neural networks. The resulting algorithm demonstrates potential benefits over traditional machine learning techniques, particularly in situations requiring nuanced optimization and rapid adaptation. This work presents a foundational investigation into the application of quantum topology for enhancing the learning process of quantum machine learning models.

title: Geometric Complexity Metrics for Robust AI Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of geometric complexity metrics to enhance the evaluation and stabilization of complex neural networks. Traditional evaluation metrics often struggle to adequately capture the intricate geometric relationships within these models, leading to unreliable assessments of robustness. We propose a novel metric, based on identifying critical points of instability, that quantifies the complexity of a neural network's geometric structure. This metric, termed "Geometric Stability Score" (GSS), offers a more robust and nuanced approach to assessing network stability, potentially leading to improved model design and training. The core mechanism involves analyzing the network's geometric properties – specifically, the presence of critical points – to identify areas where the network is particularly vulnerable to perturbations. This paper presents the implementation of the GSS, demonstrates its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and initial experiments, and discusses future research directions.

title: Microscopic Quantum Entanglement: A Non-Linear Adaptive Self-Adaptation Theory
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of microscopic quantum entanglement as a foundation for a novel non-linear adaptive self-adaptation theory for describing quantum systems. We propose a theoretical framework that leverages the unique properties of entanglement to dynamically adjust self-adaptation mechanisms, offering a pathway to optimize quantum computation's performance. This research explores the implications of entanglement-driven self-adaptation for potential quantum algorithms and computational approaches. The core claim is that this theory provides a new perspective on quantum system behavior and unlocks novel possibilities within the field of quantum computation.

title: Quantum Entanglement Coding and Neural Network Collaborative Learning
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to complex function approximation by synergistically combining Quantum Entanglement Coding (QEC) with Neural Networks (NNs). The core claim is that QEC's ability to generate rich quantum features, when coupled with the learning capabilities of NNs, can significantly enhance the efficiency of approximating complex functions. The proposed mechanism involves utilizing the output of QEC as input for an NN, leveraging the NN's strengths in pattern recognition and approximation. A feedback loop is then implemented to optimize the parameters of the QEC, iteratively improving the overall approximation performance. This work introduces a new paradigm of deep collaborative learning between quantum and classical systems, potentially unlocking solutions to challenges in areas such as machine learning and quantum computing. We demonstrate the theoretical potential of this approach and outline a framework for future research.

title: Dynamic Topology-Dependent Neural Network Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network optimization that dynamically adapts the network topology based on learned dependencies. The core idea is to leverage reinforcement learning, where two agents collaborate: one adjusts connection weights and the other modifies the network's structure (adding, removing, or restructuring connections). A 'dependency graph' guides the agents' decisions, reflecting the learned information dependencies between neurons. This dynamic adaptation addresses the limitations of traditional methods that assume a fixed network topology, particularly when dealing with complex dependencies and non-Euclidean data. The system aims to achieve more efficient training and improved generalization performance by allowing the network to evolve its structure to better represent the underlying data. The optimization process is driven by minimizing a loss function, and the dependency graph is continuously updated based on the error signal. The key contribution lies in the integration of topology adaptation with reinforcement learning, providing a framework for creating inherently adaptive and robust neural networks. The proposed methodology demonstrates potential for significant improvements in network performance across various domains.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Complexity Sorting Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel sorting algorithm based on a non-Euclidean sorting strategy. The core idea is to leverage the unique properties of non-Euclidean sets to enhance sorting efficiency. Traditional sorting algorithms often rely on simple rules, while this approach utilizes the inherent non-Euclidean characteristics of the data to optimize the sorting process. The algorithm's mechanism centers around strategically adjusting the optimization focus to align with these non-Euclidean features. This innovative approach aims to outperform conventional sorting methods in scenarios where non-Euclidean relationships play a crucial role in data structure organization. This research explores the potential of utilizing non-Euclidean properties to create a more efficient and adaptable sorting solution.

title: Adaptive Kernel Learning for Graph Representation Learning
abstract: Graph representation learning (GRL) aims to learn meaningful node embeddings from graph-structured data. Traditional approaches heavily rely on pre-defined kernel functions, a significant bottleneck in adapting to diverse graph topologies and data characteristics. This paper introduces an adaptive kernel learning algorithm that dynamically learns the optimal kernel function directly from the graph data. The algorithm iteratively refines the kernel by optimizing a loss function that reflects the desired graph structure. The key innovation lies in eliminating the manual design of kernels, enabling greater flexibility and ultimately, more effective GRL. We present a theoretical framework for understanding the algorithm and discuss its potential applications.

title: Proof Relevance Learning and Program Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program optimization based on proof relevance learning. The core idea is to automatically identify and eliminate redundancy in programs by leveraging the principles of proof relevance. We introduce a mechanism that utilizes program analysis techniques to learn irrelevant information within a program and subsequently employs this knowledge to guide optimization efforts. This approach aims to reduce code size and improve execution efficiency. The system learns by analyzing program execution paths and identifying portions that do not contribute to the overall computation. The optimization process is then driven by a proof-like argument demonstrating the irrelevance of these identified sections. This work represents a significant step towards automated and intelligent program optimization, moving beyond traditional static or dynamic analysis methods. The key contribution lies in the integration of proof relevance learning with program optimization, creating a framework for verifiable and efficient code reduction. The system's output is a modified program where redundant sections have been removed, accompanied by a formal proof of their irrelevance. ---

title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Latent State Representation
abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (Meta-RL) aims to accelerate learning across multiple tasks by learning a meta-policy that can rapidly adapt to new, unseen environments. A significant challenge in Meta-RL is sample efficiency, which stems from the need to explore diverse tasks and learn effective representations for generalization. This work proposes a novel approach to Meta-RL by incorporating a learned latent state representation. The core idea is to train a meta-learner to predict a latent state vector, effectively summarizing the relevant information from the environment's current state. This latent representation then guides the adaptive learning process, allowing the agent to quickly adapt to new tasks exhibiting similar underlying dynamics. We argue that this approach addresses the sample efficiency bottleneck by providing a compact and informative representation, thereby reducing the exploration space and improving generalization performance. The theoretical framework and the proposed mechanism are presented, highlighting the potential for enhanced Meta-RL performance.

title: 基于多模态协同推理的知识图谱查询
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to knowledge graph query answering, termed Multi-Modal Collaborative Reasoning for Knowledge Graph (MMCR-KG). The core claim is that integrating diverse data modalities, such as text, images, and potentially audio, significantly enhances query understanding and ultimately improves query accuracy within knowledge graphs. The proposed mechanism involves a framework that maps these multi-modal data streams into the knowledge graph structure and employs collaborative reasoning algorithms to fuse information from all modalities. This allows for a more comprehensive interpretation of the query intent. Experimental results (hypothetical, due to lack of experimental execution) demonstrate a potential performance gain compared to traditional text-based query approaches. This work addresses the limitations of current knowledge graph query systems, which predominantly rely on textual queries, by introducing a robust multi-modal understanding capability. The key contribution lies in the design and implementation of a flexible framework capable of handling heterogeneous data and leveraging collaborative inference to achieve superior query results. The theoretical framework is presented here, outlining the core components and their interactions.

title: Dynamic Programming for Quantum Circuit Optimization with Error Mitigation
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is a critical step in realizing the full potential of quantum computing. Traditional optimization methods often struggle to effectively balance circuit depth, gate complexity, and the inherent noise associated with quantum systems. This paper proposes a novel dynamic programming (DP) framework that integrates circuit optimization with error mitigation strategies. The core idea is to recursively explore all possible circuit transformations, incorporating error mitigation techniques as constraints within the DP search space. This approach allows for simultaneous consideration of both gate operations and error mitigation, leading to optimized circuits with reduced depth and enhanced fidelity. The algorithm is formulated as a state transition function, where each state represents a partial circuit transformation, and the objective is to minimize a cost function that combines circuit depth and an error mitigation metric. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential efficiency of this framework through a conceptual analysis and outline the key components of the implementation. Future work will focus on developing a fully optimized implementation and exploring the framework's applicability to various quantum algorithms.

abstract: This paper introduces a dynamic adaptive quantum entanglement modeling approach designed to address the challenges of accurately analyzing and predicting quantum entanglement. The core mechanism centers around employing a series of geometric transformations that are continuously refined based on the observed quantum entanglement characteristics.

title: Bigger, Better, or Just Bigger: A Interdisciplinary Mapping Review of The Scaling Laws Debate in Modern Machine Learning
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of The Scaling Laws Debate in Modern Machine Learning in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of scaling laws and compute as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Text‐based Sentiment Analysis
abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive examination of text-based sentiment analysis, the most widely studied modality. It traces the historical evolution from early lexicon- and rule-based methods to traditional machine learning approaches (such as SVM, Naive Bayes, BoW, and TF-IDF) and modern deep learning techniques, including CNNs, RNNs/LSTMs, attention mechanisms, and Transformer-based models like BERT. The chapter covers key advanced topics such as aspect-based sentiment analysis, implicit sentiment and sarcasm detection, cross-lingual challenges, and explainable AI. Detailed discussions on model architectures, training strategies, and evaluation are included. A practical case study using the IMDB movie review dataset demonstrates the performance progression from logistic regression baselines to BiLSTM and fine-tuned DistilBERT models, clearly illustrating the advantages of state-of-the-art Transformer approaches.

The chapter covers key advanced topics such as aspect-based sentiment analysis, implicit sentiment and sarcasm detection, cross-lingual challenges, and explainable AI. Detailed discussions on model architectures, training strategies, and evaluation are included. A practical case study using the IMDB movie review dataset demonstrates the performance progression from logistic regression baselines to BiLSTM and fine-tuned DistilBERT models, clearly illustrating the advantages of state-of-the-art Transformer approaches.

title: BioSync: Transformer-Based Cross-Modal Fusion for a Multimodal Physiological Digital Biomarker
abstract: Cardiac, neural, behavioral, and speech measurements from wearable and mobile devices provide partial, noise-sensitive views of physiological state. BioSync combines these measurements into the \textbf{BioSync Index (BSI)}, a continuous composite digital biomarker defined under the BEST framework. The model applies multi-head self-attention to modality tokens and adds a linear branch whose hypothesis class includes standard feature concatenation. This architecture is motivated by latent-variable measurement theory and by the possibility that joint observations contain information unavailable from individual modalities. We evaluated BioSync on two literature-informed synthetic cohorts: a four-modality cognitive-decline cohort using HRV, EEG, actigraphy, and speech, and a metabolic-autonomic cohort structured around the public AI-READI wearable schema. In the cognitive cohort, BioSync and concatenation obtained AUCs of 0.928 and 0.926, respectively. In the metabolic cohort, BioSync obtained accuracy/F1 of 0.764/0.766, compared with 0.756/0.758 for concatenation. The BSI correlated with latent severity in both cohorts ($r=0.91$ and $r=0.68$). A pure-attention ablation obtained cognitive-cohort AUC 0.911, locating the increase to 0.928 in the combined wide-and-deep architecture. With matched modality-dropout training, BioSync led concatenation at five of six cognitive-cohort corruption rates and at the highest metabolic-cohort rate. Its cognitive-cohort AUC was also higher than five published digital-biomarker reference values, although differences in datasets and tasks preclude a controlled benchmark claim. Comparison with single-modality, early-fusion, and late-fusion designs across six prespecified criteria identifies the model's computational properties; validation on real cohorts remains necessary.

title: When Seeing Overrides Knowing: Visual Dominance and Deferral-Based Method for Personalized Safety in VLMs
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, where a response that is reasonable in general may still be unsafe for a particular user whose medical, emotional, or situational context is unknown to the model. We study this problem of personalized safety in multimodal systems and introduce MPS-Bench, a benchmark of 5,181 scenarios from 584 real-world images across 12 high-risk domains, each paired with a hidden user profile. Evaluating eight frontier VLMs, we find that they almost always respond directly (86-99%) rather than seek missing context, and none exceeds 2.6/5 on personalized safety. To understand why these failures arise, we analyze multimodal interactions and identify visual dominance: visual information enters text representations early and suppresses textual risk signals during multimodal fusion. Causal interventions reveal a two-stage mechanism in which visual affect is first transferred into the text stream in early layers and then shapes the final decision through this altered text representation, making late-stage internal remediation unreliable. Motivated by this mechanism, we propose PRISM, a lightweight input monitor that uses bidirectional cross-modal modulation to predict when a query is likely to require deferral. PRISM achieves 0.978 AUC and strictly dominates the safety-utility Pareto frontier across all tested models.

title: AI-Assisted Design of a Post-Quantum Cryptographic Accelerator: A Deployed-Silicon Case Study
abstract: Post-quantum migration is mandated on published timelines, and silicon that ships with a defect cannot be patched remotely. The standard acceptance gate cannot detect an entire class of ML-DSA defects. Signing resamples until a candidate meets its norm bounds, so the executed path varies with the message, whereas known-answer tests (KATs) sample fixed values and reach only the depths their seeds trigger. Our accelerator passed its full KAT regression while carrying a norm check that outran block-RAM latency, leaving each candidate's final coefficients unverified; the escape surfaced at reject-loop iteration 5. The blind spot lies in the instrument, not the engineer; care cannot remove it. We replace that gate. A byte-exact golden-reference oracle paired with randomized adversarial soak drives the rejection loop past any fixed vector, closing the gap: 301,343 data-dependent signings, zero escapes. Because the gate judges artifacts and never authors, trust becomes separable from authorship, making AI authorship an answerable question. We report 232 logged experiments in which an agentic large language model drove a unified ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 accelerator with on-chip key custody from RTL to PCIe bring-up on one Kintex-7 XC7K160T, shipped at 98.5% slice occupancy. Success was 71.6%, following a hardware-coupling gradient, 77-85% for documentation and research against 50-53% for synthesis and bring-up, which observability can explain: failure concentrates where corrective signals are physical-side only. That so unreliable an author produced an artifact byte-exact across all six FIPS operations -- its deployed baseline surviving the same 779,945-check zero-failure soak -- is the claim.

title: Occlusion-Robust Multimodal Emotion Recognition in VR via Fusion of Facial Images and EMG
abstract: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) fundamentally limit emotion recognition in virtual reality (VR): by occluding the upper face, they render conventional image-based facial expression analysis incomplete, particularly for applications requiring real-time affective assessment. We address this challenge by fusing lower-face video with facial electromyography (EMG) from the occluded upper face to classify seven emotional categories (six basic emotions plus neutral). We introduce a synchronized multimodal dataset from 20 participants, pairing lower-face video with seven-channel upper-face EMG elicited by validated emotion stimuli. Under subject-independent test, our proposed late-fusion architecture merging convolutional visual embeddings with RBF-kernel EMG representations achieves 51% macro-F1, outperforming both image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines. These results demonstrate that upper-face EMG provides robust complementary information under HMD-induced visual occlusion and establish a foundation for multimodal emotion recognition in naturalistic VR environments. This approach facilitates affect-adaptive applications, including communication training and therapeutic interventions. The dataset will be shared upon request under an ethical-use agreement.

title: Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus
abstract: Large-language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming part of human culture, reshaping how information is produced, transmitted, and used. Here we propose that their diffusion can be understood through a viral analogy, with LLM use spreading through populations, becoming embedded in cognitive and cultural practices. We model transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and show that the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock-in. A central consequence is the possibility of runaway dynamics: once a critical threshold is crossed, small increases in adoption can trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence, with abrupt losses in cognitive competence. The same framework, however, identifies conditions for cognitive immunization, based on reducing transmission and facilitating reversibility. Our results highlight how LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with important consequences for cognitive autonomy.

title: Procedural Level Generation For 2D Platformer Games Based On Graph And Chunk
abstract: Level design is one of the key components in determining the gameplay experience in 2D platformer games. However, manual level design is time-consuming and difficult to scale. Graph theory can be used to represent the abstract structure of a level, with nodes as spatial units and edges as paths connecting those spaces. The problem is that this graph structure cannot always be directly translated into a valid and playable physical layout due to platformer constraints, such as jump height, safe distance, and gravity. This research proposes a chunk-based transformation approach, in which each graph node is represented as a fixed-size level chunk containing a platform layout, obstacles, and entry and exit points. The transformation of the graph into a physical level is carried out through the selection, arrangement, and alignment of chunks based on the graph’s topology. This study aims to design a framework for transforming an abstract graph G=(V,E) into a chunk-based 2D platformer level layout. The method used is qualitative-descriptive, involving the formulation of a graph model, rules for mapping and arranging chunks, and playability criteria. The results of the study reveal three main stages: mapping vertices to corresponding chunks, arranging chunks according to the graph’s structure, and validating reachability using an automatic path-finding agent.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Topology for Quantum Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm design based on adaptive quantum topology. Traditional algorithm design relies on classical approaches, while this work leverages the unique properties of quantum topology to enhance algorithm efficiency. The core mechanism involves constructing a quantum circuit that exploits topological features to achieve specific computational goals. This research explores the potential of quantum topology for algorithm optimization, presenting a new framework for designing quantum solutions to complex problems. The paper details the algorithm's design, theoretical analysis, and initial experimental validation. The core claim is that the proposed algorithm offers significant improvements in algorithm efficiency compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving topological constraints.

title: Title: Quantum Error Mitigation via Non-Gaussian Noise Distribution
abstract: Quantum computing promises revolutionary computational capabilities, but its inherent fragility necessitates robust error mitigation strategies. Conventional error correction schemes often fall short, struggling to effectively address the complex noise patterns within quantum systems. This paper proposes a novel method for quantum error mitigation centered around the design of a specifically tailored non-Gaussian noise distribution. We hypothesize that this distribution, by actively suppressing errors, can significantly enhance the fidelity of quantum computations. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging the non-Gaussian characteristics of the noise to create a more resilient and effective error correction process. This work presents a preliminary investigation into the potential benefits of this approach and outlines a pathway toward future advancements in quantum error mitigation.

title: Quantum-Inspired Constraint Optimization via Hybrid Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired neural networks to constraint optimization, aiming to address the limitations of traditional optimization methods when faced with complex, high-dimensional problems. We propose a novel hybrid approach that integrates quantum-inspired neural networks into the optimization process, leveraging their ability to capture subtle patterns and relationships within the problem space. The goal is to significantly improve the performance of constraint optimization, particularly in scenarios where conventional methods fall short. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing the neural network to generate a surrogate model that facilitates faster and more efficient search, enabling the solution of challenging problems. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in optimization speed and accuracy compared to existing methods, especially when dealing with intricate constraint formulations.

title: Title: Non-Local Quantum Entanglement for Sensor Networks
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing sensor networks. This paper explores the design and implementation of a sensor network leveraging non-local quantum entanglement to achieve enhanced accuracy and resilience in distributed sensing. The core claim centers on utilizing quantum repeaters to extend the range of entangled photons, creating a network capable of processing information across significant distances. We address the challenges associated with maintaining entanglement fidelity in a network setting and propose a novel approach to overcome these hurdles, ultimately demonstrating a prototype sensor network demonstrating enhanced accuracy and resilience compared to traditional methods. We will delve into the theoretical underpinnings of entanglement-based communication, the role of quantum repeaters, and the potential implications for a wide range of sensing applications.

title: Relational Memory Networks with Episodic Recurrence
abstract: This paper introduces Relational Memory Networks with Episodic Recurrence (RMNER), a novel architecture designed to address the limitations of existing memory networks regarding episodic memory representation and retrieval. Traditional memory networks struggle to effectively utilize the temporal context of events, leading to difficulties in tasks requiring reasoning based on past interactions. RMNER overcomes this challenge by integrating a recurrent mechanism within the memory network. This recurrent architecture creates and maintains a "memory trace" representing the chronological order and relationships between past events. This memory trace is then leveraged to guide future retrieval and reasoning processes, effectively mimicking the dynamics of episodic memory. We posit that this explicit incorporation of temporal context offers a significant advancement in memory network capabilities, enabling more sophisticated and context-aware reasoning. The core of this approach lies in the recurrent connections within the memory network, allowing for the persistent representation and manipulation of temporal information. This paper details the architecture, the underlying mathematical framework, and demonstrates the potential of RMNER through a theoretical analysis.

title: Graph Attention Networks with Memory-Augmented Attention
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to Graph Attention Networks (GATs) that addresses a critical limitation of the original architecture: the inability to effectively retain and utilize information from previously attended nodes. We propose a memory-augmented attention mechanism that integrates a short-term memory component into the GAT framework. This memory stores contextual information about nodes that have been previously attended, allowing the attention mechanism to consider the broader graph context when determining node importance. Our approach improves the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and enhances performance on tasks requiring a comprehensive understanding of graph structures. The core idea is to provide GATs with a historical perspective, mitigating the issue of solely focusing on immediate neighbors. We present a detailed formulation of the augmented attention mechanism and demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples. The key mathematical components are defined below.

title: Cognitive Graph Dynamics – Predictive Bayesian Inference at Scale
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for modeling cognitive processes based on dynamic graph evolution driven by predictive Bayesian inference. The core idea is that human-like cognition can be represented by evolving, dynamically weighted graphs. Nodes in this graph represent concepts, and edges represent probabilistic relationships between them. The system utilizes a massively parallel architecture to simulate this graph, continuously updating its structure and weights through distributed Bayesian inference. Incoming sensory data and internal predictions serve as the primary drivers for graph evolution. This approach differs from traditional cognitive modeling by explicitly incorporating dynamic graph evolution, mimicking the adaptive and contextual nature of human thought. The key mathematical formulation centers around probabilistic graphical models, with updates governed by Bayesian inference equations. The system's architecture emphasizes scalability and efficiency, enabling the simulation of complex cognitive phenomena at a level comparable to human performance. Specifically, the framework leverages Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for inference and incorporates a Laplacian smoothing technique to handle uncertainty in edge weight estimation. The potential impact of this research lies in developing more accurate and computationally tractable models of human cognition, with applications in areas such as artificial intelligence, robotics, and neuroscience.

title: GKOS v0.81 — A Developmental Pre-standard for AI Governance, Accountability and Auditability
abstract: Governed Knowledge Operations Standard (GKOS), developmental specification / public working draft. Documentation patch v0.82.1 clarifies publication status and existing exact-bound claims controls. The project name, titles and identifiers are retained. Technical requirements, schemas, runner behavior, GKX 2.0, 62 permanent allocations and 28 gate codes are unchanged from v0.82. R23 remains prospective; no profile is qualified and no implementation claim carries forward automatically. Owner-authorized, non-consensus and non-qualifying. Public GitHub visibility, signatures, CI and archival do not establish standards maturity, certification or regulatory acceptance. Documentation and original graphics are CC BY 4.0; schemas, fixtures, workflows, scripts and reference code remain Apache-2.0. Metadata is prepared before publication; the public release timestamp and verified archive establish actual publication.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Distributed Key Generation Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel protocol for distributed key generation (DKG) leveraging quantum entanglement. The core claim is to demonstrate the secure and efficient generation of a shared secret key among multiple parties using the unique properties of entangled quantum states. The protocol utilizes a specifically designed entangled state shared between the participating nodes. This shared state facilitates the synchronous generation of keys across the distributed network. The key innovation lies in the enhanced security provided by the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics, eliminating the vulnerabilities inherent in classical DKG protocols susceptible to eavesdropping attacks. Furthermore, the protocol aims to improve key generation efficiency by utilizing the inherent correlations present within the entangled state. We detail the mathematical formulation of the protocol, including the state preparation, entanglement distribution, and key extraction phases. The proposed approach offers a promising direction for secure communication in quantum networks.

title: Neuromorphic Spiking Reservoir Computing for Real-Time Object Tracking
abstract: This paper investigates the application of spiking reservoir computing (SRC) for real-time object tracking, leveraging the inherent temporal processing capabilities of spiking neural networks. The core claim is that optimized SRC parameters can achieve high accuracy and low latency in tracking moving objects. The proposed system utilizes a dynamically adjusted spiking reservoir network to process visual data, effectively capturing temporal dependencies crucial for object tracking. The methodology focuses on tailoring reservoir parameters – synaptic scaling, excitability, and input scaling – to minimize latency and maximize tracking performance. Mathematical formulations detail the dynamics of the reservoir, the input-output relationship, and the optimization strategies employed. The results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, showcasing its potential for applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and surveillance systems. The key innovations lie in the dynamic adaptation of the reservoir parameters and the explicit integration of temporal processing principles within an SRC framework.

title: Title: Boolean Network Formalism for Cognitive Processes
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Boolean network theory to model and analyze cognitive processes, proposing a novel refinement of the core logic to incorporate emergent behavior – a key component of complex cognitive systems. We explore how this expansion can allow for a more nuanced and accurate simulation of decision-making and reasoning, offering a mathematically precise framework for understanding how cognitive networks generate unexpected outcomes. The core mechanism centers on the evolution of Boolean network structures through interaction, leading to emergent properties that deviate from simple rule-based predictions. This paper will detail the methodology, initial results, and potential applications of this approach.

title: Emergent Program Synthesis (EPS)
abstract: Emergent Program Synthesis (EPS) presents a novel approach to automated program generation by leveraging evolutionary algorithms to explore the vast space of possible program solutions. This work details a framework utilizing a genetic algorithm to iteratively synthesize programs, mimicking the process of biological evolution. The core mechanism involves encoding program code as genetic material, employing crossover, mutation, and selection operations to generate new candidate programs. These candidates are evaluated through interaction with a target problem's testing environment, with successful programs being retained and propagated through subsequent generations. The system's capacity to uncover solutions outside of pre-defined templates distinguishes it from conventional program synthesis techniques. The primary goal is to achieve complex program generation with minimal human intervention. This paper outlines the fundamental principles, design choices, and potential of the EPS framework.

title: 基于图卷积神经网络的社交网络分析
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs) for social network analysis. Traditional methods for analyzing social networks often struggle to capture complex relationships and patterns within the network structure. GCNs offer a powerful approach by directly leveraging the graph-structured nature of social networks. We present a framework for utilizing GCNs to learn node representations based on the network topology and node features. These learned representations can then be used for various downstream tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and community detection. The core claim of this work is to demonstrate the effectiveness of GCNs in revealing social relationships and behavior patterns within social networks. The mechanism involves transforming the social network into a graph, applying GCNs to learn node connections and patterns, and predicting node behavior. This research contributes to the expansion of graph neural network applications and enhances the analytical capabilities for social network data. The primary goal is to provide a robust and effective method for extracting meaningful insights from complex social network data.

title: Space-Time Network Computation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel network computation model termed "Space-Time Network Computation" (STNC). The core claim is that integrating spatial and temporal dimensions offers a more efficient approach to processing data exhibiting spatial and temporal dependencies. STNC leverages an extension of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by introducing the concepts of time streams and spatial streams. These streams are utilized within a graph structure to simulate and compute spatial-temporal interactions. The fundamental innovation lies in overcoming the dimensional limitations of traditional network computations, providing a new paradigm for handling complex spatial-temporal data. This approach utilizes graph structures to represent relationships, incorporating temporal evolution through time streams and spatial relationships through spatial streams. The key mathematical formulation is presented as follows: Let *G* = (*V*, *E*) be a graph, where *V* represents the set of nodes (vertices) and *E* represents the set of edges. Each node *vi* ∈ *V* is associated with a state vector *si* ∈ ℝd, where *d* is the dimension of the state vector. Each edge *eij* ∈ *E* is characterized by a weight *wij* ≥ 0. A *time stream* τ is defined as a sequence of state vectors: τ = (*si(0)*, *si(1)*, *si(2)*, ..., *si(T)*) , where *si(t)* is the state vector of node *i* at time *t*. A *spatial stream* σ is defined as a set of state vectors representing the spatial neighborhood of a node: σ(*i*) = {*sj(t)* | (*j*, *i*) ∈ *E*} for each node *i*. The core computation within STNC involves updating node states based on their time streams and spatial streams. The update rule can be expressed as: *si(t+1)* = f(*si(t)*, τi, σ(*i*)) where *f* is an update function, τi is the time stream associated with node *i*, and σ(*i*) is the spatial stream for node *i*. This update function can be a neural network or a more traditional rule-based system. The goal is to iteratively evolve the state vectors of nodes over time, capturing the influence of their neighbors and the temporal dynamics. The effectiveness of STNC is predicated on the efficient representation and manipulation of these time streams and spatial streams within the graph structure. The choice of *f* is crucial and will be explored in subsequent sections. The proposed model offers a flexible framework capable of accommodating diverse spatial-temporal data and associated dynamics. Further research will focus on optimizing the update function *f* and exploring its applicability to various domains.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Vector Space Analysis for Cryptographic Resilience
abstract: This paper explores the application of non-Euclidean vector spaces to enhance cryptographic resilience. Traditional cryptographic methods often rely on the assumption of Euclidean space, but this assumption may be insufficient for certain scenarios. We propose a novel method for quantifying the resilience of cryptographic algorithms to non-Euclidean transformations, leveraging advanced mathematical tools to identify vulnerabilities. This research aims to broaden the scope of vulnerability assessment beyond conventional approaches by incorporating geometric properties previously overlooked. The core mechanism involves constructing a new metric for evaluating resilience, providing a rigorous framework for understanding and mitigating potential weaknesses. This work demonstrates the potential of non-Euclidean geometry to significantly improve the security of cryptographic systems.

title: 基于量子自旋的拓扑数据压缩
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum spin systems to data compression, specifically focusing on the development of a novel data compression technique based on the adaptive topology of quantum spin states. We propose a method that leverages the inherent properties of quantum spin to construct and manipulate data, resulting in enhanced compression efficiency compared to conventional methods. The core of our approach involves designing a data structure that utilizes quantum spin states to dynamically adjust the data's representation, optimizing for storage and retrieval. This research explores the potential of quantum phenomena to revolutionize data compression, offering a paradigm shift in data storage strategies. The proposed method demonstrates significant improvements in compression ratios, particularly for data with complex patterns, and provides a foundation for future advancements in data compression technology.

title: 基于自适应的量子纠缠数据压缩
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental quantum phenomenon, offers the potential for unparalleled data compression. However, harnessing this potential requires sophisticated techniques to manage the delicate quantum states involved. This paper introduces a novel data compression algorithm based on adaptive quantum entanglement management, aiming to significantly enhance compression efficiency compared to existing approaches. The core mechanism centers around dynamically adjusting key entanglement parameters during the compression process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and experiments, showcasing a substantial improvement in data compression ratios. The algorithm leverages the inherent properties of entanglement to optimize data representation and minimize redundancy, offering a promising path towards practical quantum data storage and transmission.

title: Student Feedback Analysis Using Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing: A Real-Time Web-Based System
abstract: Student feedback is a critical component for enhancing teaching quality, refining curriculum design, and supporting institutional improvement in modern education. However, manually analyzing large volumes of feedback is time-consuming and often influenced by subjective interpretation. The objective of this research is to design and implement an automated sentiment analysis system that classifies student feedback as positive, negative, or neutral, thereby enabling educational institutions to make timely, data-driven decisions. The proposed solution is a web-based application that integrates NLP and ML techniques. HTML, CSS and JavaScript is used to design the front-end and Python-Flask is used as a back-end. The collected feedback was processed with the help of tokenisation, stemming, stop-word removal, and TF-IDF-based feature extraction techniques. Two classifiers, Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Multinomial Naive Bayes, were trained and evaluated on a labelled dataset. Performance metrics such as F1-score, recall, accuracy, and precision were used for evaluation. The results indicate that SVM outperformed the other models with an accuracy of 85%, establishing the system as a practical tool for real-time sentiment monitoring in the classroom.

title: Conclusion and Outlook
abstract: This concluding chapter synthesizes the major insights presented throughout the book. It revisits the technological evolution of sentiment analysis from rule-based systems to cognitive intelligence powered by large language models. The practical value of sentiment analysis across diverse domains is summarized through a four-stage value chain (listen, understand, predict, and respond). A structured examination of ethical risks, including algorithmic bias, emotional manipulation, and privacy invasion, is provided, accompanied by a multi-level mitigation framework. Promising future research directions are outlined, focusing on causal inference, explainable AI, synergistic integration with generative AI, and human-computer collaboration. The chapter emphasizes the importance of responsible governance and the ultimate goal of developing affective intelligence that serves humanity with fairness and empathy.

title: Fractional-Order Adaptive Motion Magnification: Phase-Reliability Weighting for Noise-Constrained Video Amplification
abstract: Eulerian video amplification boosts sub-pixel motion by band-pass filtering per-pixel intensity traces and applying a uniform gain. That gain ignores local structure, so sensor noise is amplified together with the signal, especially in textureless regions where the monogenic phase is unreliable. We propose FrAM (Fractional-order Adaptive Motion Magnification), a pipeline developed first offline and then as a causal stream. It replaces the constant temporal gain with a Grünwald--Letnikov derivative of fractional order, giving continuous control over high-frequency emphasis, and replaces the uniform spatial gain with a per-pixel weight derived from the local amplitude of the monogenic signal. On a controlled synthetic sequence split into textured and flat halves, FrAM matches the amplification of the Eulerian baseline while keeping flat-region temporal noise at the input level. The reduction holds across an eightfold range of input noise levels. Real videos show improved spatial selectivity and lower background noise in every case. The causal reformulation cuts the per-frame cost by two orders of magnitude, reaching 69\,fps at 640$\times$480.
